stem: Which of the following Indian leaders attended the First Round Table Conference in London?
expl: On 10 June and 24 June 1930, the Simon Commission’s report was published in two parts. Indian political organizations rejected the Commission’s recommendations. At the time the report was published, the main Congress leaders were in jail. In an atmosphere of disappointment and dissatisfaction, the British government convened the First Round Table Conference in London in November 1930. About 89 representatives participated, but no representative from the Congress attended. The prominent Indian participants included—Tej Bahadur Sapru, V. S. Srinivasa Sastri, Muhammad Ali, Muhammad Shafi, Aga Khan, Fazlul Haq, Muhammad Ali Jinnah, Homi Modi, M. R. Jayakar, Moonje, B. R. Ambedkar, and Sundar Singh Majithia.

stem: Who participated in all three Round Table Conferences?
expl: Among the given options, the Dalit leader B. R. Ambedkar participated in all the three Round Table Conferences. In the Second Round Table Conference, Mahatma Gandhi took part as the sole representative of the Congress. Besides him, Sarojini Naidu and Madan Mohan Malaviya also participated in this conference.

stem: Which Round Table Conference was held in 1932?
expl: The First Round Table Conference was held in London from 12 November 1930 to 19 January 1931. Representatives of the Indian Liberal Party, Muslim League, Hindu Mahasabha, Depressed Classes, business community, and princely states participated, but the Congress did not join it. The Second Round Table Conference was held in London from 7 September 1931 to 1 December 1931, in which Gandhi participated as the sole representative of the Congress. The Third Round Table Conference was held in London from 17 November 1932 to 24 December 1932. The Congress boycotted this conference.

stem: On which issue did the Second Round Table Conference fail?

options.label: c
options.text: The date of transfer of ruling power

expl: The Second Round Table Conference began on 7 September 1931, in which Mahatma Gandhi participated as the sole representative of the Congress. Due to disputes over the communal issue, the conference could not reach any decisive conclusion. Dalit leader B. R. Ambedkar demanded separate electorates for Dalits, which Gandhi rejected. Ultimately, due to the deadlock over communal representation, the conference was declared closed on 1 December 1931.

stem: Mahatma Gandhi returned to India in December, 1931 empty-handed from
expl: As the sole representative of the Congress, Mahatma Gandhi participated in the Second Round Table Conference, which began on 7 September, 1931. However, on 28 December, 1931, he returned from London to Bombay, disappointed and empty-handed. On reaching India, he said, “It is true that I have returned empty-handed, but I am satisfied that the flag which was entrusted to me, I did not let it fall, and I did not compromise with its honour.”

stem: Who was the Prime Minister of England at the time of the Round Table Conference?
expl: To discuss constitutional reforms in India, the British government organized three Round Table Conferences during 1930–32 as part of a series of conferences. These conferences were conducted on the basis of the report submitted by the Simon Commission in June, 1930. At this time, James Ramsay MacDonald was the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom.

stem: A separate electoral group was made by the Communal Award of Ramsay MacDonald first time in August, 1932 for–
expl: British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald presented the Communal Award on 16 August, 1932. Under it, certain seats were reserved in the legislatures for each minority community, and the members were to be elected through separate electorates. Muslims and Sikhs were already considered minorities. Now, under this Communal Award, the Dalit class was also treated as a minority and separated from the Hindus.

stem: How many seats were given to Depressed Classes under Communal Award and Poona Pact?
expl: In the Communal Award, the number of reserved seats for Dalits in the provincial legislatures was 71, which was increased in the Poona Pact (Poona Agreement) to 148 (Madras–30; Bombay including Sindh–15; Punjab–8; Bihar and Orissa–18; Central Provinces and Berar–20; Assam–7; Bengal–30; and the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh–20). In some books, however, this number is given as 147. Also, in the Central Legislature, 18 percent of the seats from the general category were reserved for the Dalit classes.
